title: Castle-in-the-Air: Probing the Foundational Visual Deficits of MLLMs via Bottom-Up Cognitive Factors
claim: Even the best frontier models fall well short of the human baseline on foundational visual abilities, with uneven strengths across cognitive domains.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right ranked stacked bars, legend top-right, human bar leftmost
description: A single wide stacked bar chart ranks about 40 models from left to right by overall score. The y-axis is Performance (%), running from 0 to over 300 because the four domain scores are summed. Each bar is split into four colors: blue for Visualization & Spatial, red for Perceptual & Closure, green for Memory, and yellow for Reasoning. A legend sits in the top-right corner. The leftmost bar is the Human baseline, at about 310 and clearly the tallest. The proprietary models Gemini-3.1-Pro and GPT-5.5 come next at about 245. After that the bars decline steadily down to tiny bars for LLaMA-3.2 Vision models. Model names are on rotated x-axis labels. The eye goes first to the tall Human bar and then follows the descending staircase of bars.
caption: A stacked bar chart ranks all models by overall score, with each bar decomposed into the four cognitive domains. There is still a gap between the best model and our human baseline (average performance of undergraduate students). Figure [ref] further shows model scores vs. their release dates.
abstract: Humans develop perception through a bottom-up hierarchy: from basic primitives and Gestalt principles to high-level semantics. Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are trained directly on complex downstream tasks. Does it guarantee their performance on these foundational visual capabilities? To systematically investigate this gap, we introduce VisFacor, a benchmark that digitizes 20 vision-centric subtests from FRCT, a well-established cognitive psychology assessment spanning four domains of human visual cognition. Furthermore, we design algorithms to automatically construct and validate unlimited test cases with controllable difficulty. Using VisFacor, we evaluate 39 frontier MLLMs, including both proprietary (e.g., GPT, Gemini) and open-source (e.g., LLaMA, Qwen) models. The best model achieves a score of only 55.9%. Analysis reveals good internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.94) and construct validity (compared to existing vision benchmarks). Models consistently fail on tasks such as mental rotation, spatial relation inference, and figure-ground discrimination, regardless of model size or prompting strategy. These findings suggest that performance improvements on existing general benchmarks might represent castles in the air instead of a genuine mastery of human-like visual cognition.
